teacher:
Opening (2 min)

Goal: To name the real situation the lesson prepares and to set the outcome as five things she can say, not a length she has to fill.

Run it: Read the subtitle aloud, then ask what she already knows about the visit. Two or three exchanges.

Check: Can she say, in her own words, what today produces?

If needed: If she starts on the whole presentation, say that today is the opening only.

Move on when: The scope is clear to her.

Your first minute (3 min)

Goal: To fix the interlocutor, the moment, the outcome and the support before any language is taught.

Run it: Go through the six lines. Stop on Support and say it plainly: the slide and the speech map stay in front of her, today and on the day.

Check: Ask her to name the five things the opening has to do. The list is on the next screens; she does not need it from memory.

If needed: If she asks how many visitors there will be, say that only the president is confirmed. Do not supply a number — and show her that not knowing is itself something she can say.

Move on when: She can state what a successful opening looks like.

What makes this hard (5 min)

Goal: To name the four risks before they happen, so that the toolkit in stage 4 answers something she has already recognized.

Run it: Read the four rows. Then ask the question at the bottom and let her choose one.

Check: Her choice is diagnostic — write it down, with the reason she gives.

If needed: If she says all four, ask which one has actually happened to her.

Move on when: She has chosen one and said why. Do not give the repair language here: naming the risk is this stage, the language is stage 4.

First version (5 min)

Goal: To obtain an unmodelled sample of her opening, which is the diagnostic instrument of the whole block.

Run it: Set the scene in one sentence, then stop talking. Do not correct, do not prompt, do not finish her sentences. Do not interrupt for errors that do not block communication. Write down what she says, in her own words — you will use three of her lines in stage 7 and in lesson 2.

Check: Which of the five functions appear on their own, and which do not appear at all. If she pauses after an unknown word, observe how she attempts to recover, and whether the sentence continues.

If needed: If she stops completely, wait a few seconds before helping. The recovery is the evidence.

Move on when: She has produced something, however short. Do not ask for a second attempt here.

A clear, simple opening (3 min)

Goal: To let her compare her own version with a plain model, and to find the five functions rather than the words.

Run it: Let her read it silently first. Then ask the question at the bottom.

Check: Can she name at least one difference between the model and her version? If she names a difference in vocabulary only, ask what the model does that hers did not.

If needed: If she says the model is too simple, agree — simple is what survives at speed.

Optional: If she did the pre-class, say that this is the same text she read; it is meant to come back.

Move on when: She has named at least one difference.

Five lines (6 min)

Goal: To install five reusable chunks, one per communicative function, and to fix the stress of the three words that carry the message.

Run it: Say each line once at natural speed, then once slowly. She repeats. Then change one element and have her say it again — identical repetition does not count as practice.

Check: Can she locate and produce each line with the speech map available? If line 3 breaks, split it into three and rebuild it.

If needed: If have been is unstable, do not teach the present perfect. Treat the line as one block: we-have-been-in-the-healthcare-market-for.

Optional: If the three stress patterns are already stable, drop the pronunciation box and give the time to line 3.

Move on when: She can produce lines 1, 2 and 5 on request, with or without consulting the map.

When something goes wrong (3 min)

Goal: To give her four short moves that keep the interaction alive when the language fails.

Run it: One line each, said out loud. Then interrupt her with a fast question and have her use move 1 or move 4.

Check: Two of the four used under interruption, without an apology in front of them. Move 4 is the one that protects the facts: an unconfirmed company figure is never completed or invented — not by her, and not by you.

If needed: If only one move is retained, prioritize move 2, because it helps her redirect questions outside her responsibility.

Move on when: She has used two of them under interruption.

Change one thing (5 min)

Goal: To make the five lines flexible rather than memorized, by changing one element at a time.

Run it: Six changes, no more. You name the change, she says the line. Keep the pace fast — this is drilling, not discussion.

Check: Does the message remain clear when one element changes? If line 3 breaks when the order changes, rebuilding it is the practice.

If needed: If she is losing the thread, drop to three changes and drill those to fluency instead.

Move on when: She can use the correct line after each prompt, with or without consulting the map. Every repetition must change something: the audience, the model, or the starting point.

Essential message, then details (5 min)

Goal: To build the opening by content, adding functions one at a time rather than filling a duration.

Run it: First pass with lines 1, 2 and 5 — the company, the time in the market, her role. Then add lines 3 and 4. The map stays visible in both passes, and it stays available in the retask too — consulting it is an authorized strategy, not a failure.

Check: Does the second pass add the two functions without losing the three she already had?

If needed: If the expanded version breaks down, go back to the three lines and add only one.

Move on when: She has completed one pass with all five functions, however imperfect.

The opening, for real (9 min)

Goal: To run the main production of the lesson under the real conditions of the visit, without interruption.

Run it: Play the visitor. Greet her, then let her open. Do not correct during the production. When she finishes, ask the three questions on the screen.

Check: Which of the five functions arrived, and what happened at the first hesitation. Note her exact words — stage 7 is built from what you actually hear.

If needed: Intervene only on complete communication breakdown, or on a factual error about the company — an error that does not block communication is noted, not interrupted. Nothing else.

Optional: The fourth question — Which areas do you oversee? — is behind the follow-up control on this screen. Open it only if the first three went well: it invites a list.

Move on when: She has opened once and answered at least two questions.

What just happened, and once more (7 min)

Goal: To return one thing that worked and one thing that would change the message, and to have her say the corrected stretch straight after building it.

Run it: Type into the board in front of her, choosing the point from the production you actually heard. Then go to the block at the bottom and have her say only that stretch. The Clearer version stays on the screen while she says it.

Check: The two top fields are the same data the student sees in her Feedback tab — what you write there reaches her, and nothing else on this screen does. In the retask, does the change hold? Consulting the Clearer version while she says it is an authorized strategy, not a failure.

If needed: If nothing needs changing, say so and go straight to the closing. An invented correction is worse than none. If she asks to run the whole opening again, allow it after the short one.

Optional: Her first version is behind the control below the board; open it only if quoting her own words back helps.

Move on when: The corrected stretch has been said once more.

Close (2 min)

Goal: To confirm what was worked on today and to name the continuity into lesson 2.

Run it: Read the three blocks. Then close the lesson with Finish lesson in the bar below.

Check: Nothing. This screen registers, it does not test — a partial lesson is still a lesson, and the closing has to be true in that case too.

If needed: If a function did not appear today, say which one carries into the next lesson instead of marking it missing.

Move on when: The lesson is closed.
